question: Why do our cold B2B emails land in Gmail's SPAM folder with the banner 'It's similar to messages that were identified as spam' despite verified-perfect SPF/DKIM/DMARC on warmed Google Workspace domains — and what is the evidence-based, myth-busted ruleset for cold-email copy that reliably reaches the Gmail Primary inbox? Apply it to diagnose and rewrite our specific Email 1.
context: B2B cold email to US roofing contractors via Instantly. Google Workspace sending domains; SPF + DKIM + DMARC verified perfect (DMARC p=reject); mailboxes warmed; plain text; no open/link tracking; NO links or images in Email 1. A Gmail seed test landed in SPAM with the CONTENT-pattern banner 'It's similar to messages that were identified as spam' (NOT a domain-reputation banner, NOT an auth failure). EMAIL 1 VERBATIM: 'Hey [firstName], this is Joe. Just took a look at [companyName]'s site — noticed a few things Google is penalizing you for: [3 bulleted findings, e.g. No location pages (service area unverified) / No storm damage page / No manufacturer pages]. Also a handful of other technical issues (rebuild territory). These issues typically cost you about 1-2 jobs a week, give or take. Let me know if you want to see what a rebuild would look like — I've got a demo you can check out. Joe'. The email leads with an SEO-audit findings list and a loss/fear frame, sent near-identically (merge-var personalized) to thousands.
subQuestions: What does Gmail's 'similar to messages that were identified as spam' signal specifically mean — content fingerprinting / ML content classifiers / bulk-pattern detection vs IP/domain reputation flags — and can a message with perfect SPF/DKIM/DMARC still be spam-foldered purely on content/pattern?

Which specific content patterns, phrases, words, structures, and formatting actually trigger spam classification in cold email, separating evidence-backed factors from debunked 'spam trigger word list' folklore?

How much does template fingerprinting (near-identical content sent to thousands) hurt inbox placement, and how much do spintax / content randomization / per-message uniqueness measurably help? Cite real benchmarks where they exist.
How do recipient engagement signals (replies, 'mark not spam', opens, delete-without-open) and the cold-start reputation problem drive Gmail folder placement (Primary vs Promotions vs Spam)?

What do credible deliverability authorities (Instantly, Smartlead, lemlist, Quickmail, MailReach, GlockApps, Google Postmaster guidance, Mailmodo) actually recommend for inbox-safe cold-email copy — ideal length, structure, first line, CTA type, link policy, personalization depth, what to never include?

Is 'I audited your website / here are your SEO problems / let me rebuild it' web-design/SEO cold outreach an especially heavily spam-filtered category, and what specifically gets that category into the inbox?

How do you scientifically test and iterate inbox placement (seed tests, GlockApps/MailReach, controlled one-variable changes, attribution), and given OUR exact profile (perfect auth + warmed Google Workspace + a CONTENT-pattern spam flag) what is the single highest-leverage fix plus the full rank-ordered list of changes?
checklist: Meaning of Gmail's content-similarity spam signal vs domain/IP reputation vs auth; whether perfect auth can still spam-folder on content alone
Evidence-backed content spam triggers vs debunked spam-word-list myths
Template fingerprinting and content variation/spintax impact on placement (with benchmarks if available)
Engagement signals and cold-start reputation in Primary/Promotions/Spam placement
Authority best-practice ruleset for inbox-safe cold-email copy
SEO/website-audit cold-outreach category — spam risk and what inboxes it
Scientific placement testing and iteration methodology
Ranked diagnosis of OUR Email 1 (what trips the filter, in order) + prescribed rewrite direction preserving the diagnostic/loss-framing strategy
stopCondition: Each competing placement-cause hypothesis (content-pattern vs domain reputation vs engagement/cold-start) supported by >=2 independent credible sources; the anti-spam copy ruleset and the ranked fix for our profile grounded only in adversarially-verified claims; spam-word-list folklore explicitly flagged as myth where the evidence refutes it.
